title: Russian verbs in a nutshell: aspect, conjugation, -ся

blocks.text: A short tour of the Russian verb — the infinitive, the two ways of conjugating it, the past tense, aspect and the ending -ся — before the course takes the conjugation types one by one.
The infinitive and the six forms
The Russian infinitive (such a form as "to read", "to speak", "to know") usually ends in **-ть**: **читать** (to read), **говорить** (to speak). In dictionaries verbs are given in the infinitive.
DLI Grammar Reference Book, Lesson 15.

Russian has two words for 'you' like French and German, but unlike modern English. Briefly, **ты** is used informally for a single person who you know well, while **вы** is used for groups of people, or for an individual person to whom you want to show respect.
The infinitive almost always ends in **-ть**, and conjugating a verb is as simple as removing this **-ть** and adding the appropriate ending.
Wikibooks, Russian — Grammar/Verbs (CC BY-SA 4.0).
Two basic types of conjugation

Russian verbs may be divided into two basic groups according to their personal endings in the present tense. The present tense has six forms which are used with the corresponding personal pronouns. The 1st type of conjugation is characterized by the vowel **е** (**ё** if accented): the second type is characterized by the vowel **и**.
DLI Grammar Reference Book, Lesson 15.

blocks.text: If you're using the perfective aspect to form the future, simply conjugate it as you would the imperfective aspect, and this creates the future tense.
Wikibooks, Russian — Grammar/Verbs (CC BY-SA 4.0).
The past tense

To form the past tense of either aspect of a verb, remove the ending **-ть**, and add **-л**. If the subject of the verb is feminine, add **-ла**. If it is neuter, add **-ло**, and if it is plural, add **-ли**.
Wikibooks, Russian — Grammar/Past tense (CC BY-SA 4.0).
Thus, the past does not have special endings for each person, but shows the gender and the number.
DLI Grammar Reference Book, Lesson 36.
Aspect
In Russian almost every action is expressed by a pair of verbs. Such twin-verbs differ only in what we call aspect, and otherwise have the same basic meaning.
The imperfective aspect emphasizes the action itself. The perfective aspect places the emphasis on the result of the action.

The verb **написать** is called perfective and expresses a single action with emphasis on its completion (either in the past or in the future, since the present tense deals only with actions in progress).
DLI Grammar Reference Book, Lesson 37. The Verbal Aspect lessons later in this course take it further.
Verbs in -ся
Reflexive verbs. These verbs express an action which is directed back upon the agent or subject: *Я моюсь. Мы готовимся к экзамену.*
DLI Grammar Reference Book, Lessons 66–67.
Note that, as in the present tense, we use **-ся** if the word ends in a consonant, and **-сь** if it ends in a vowel.
Wikibooks, Russian — Grammar/Past tense (CC BY-SA 4.0).
How this course goes

items: Each module is a **chart page** with no exercises, then **practice pages** with verbs of that type only. Each exercise names the verb, its aspect, tense and person, and after the answer the note shows every form of the verb.

The types are the sixteen of Zaliznyak's classification, numbered as in Wiktionary's Appendix:Russian verbs: 1 -ать, -ять, -еть; 2 -овать, -евать; 3 -нуть; 4 -ить; 5 -еть, -ать (и-type); 6 -ать (stem change); 7 -ти, -сть, -зть; 8 -чь; 9 -ереть; 10 -олоть, -ороть; 11 -ить (пью); 12 -ыть, -уть, -еть; 13 -авать; 14 -ять, -ать (нять, мять, жать, чать); 15 -ть (стану); 16 -ть (живу).
Reflexive verbs have a module of their own after the first two types; position verbs follow type 5; the irregular verbs of the site's own list are the large module after type 16.
Then Verbal Aspect, and Verb Forms and Participles: the imperative, the conditional, the participles and the деепричастия.
